metadata.title: Lower urinary tract symptoms in men: management
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the assessment and management of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in men over 18. It covers initial and specialist assessment, conservative measures, drug treatment, surgery and management of urinary retention. Its aim is to improve quality of life by identifying when each approach may help.

toxicities.event: Serum sodium below the normal range
recognition: Measure serum sodium 3 days after the first dose.

management.severity: Serum sodium below the normal range

toxicities.dose_modifications: Stop desmopressin if serum sodium falls below the normal range.

conditions.name: lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
conditions.description: Symptoms affecting urine storage, voiding or the period after micturition. Possible sources include the prostate, urethra, bladder and sphincters; other potential causes include detrusor dysfunction, prostatitis, urinary tract infection, prostate cancer and neurological disease.
conditions.epidemiology: Age is an important risk factor, and prevalence rises as men get older. Bothersome symptoms affect up to 30% of men older than 65 years.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms can substantially impair quality of life and may indicate serious urogenital disease, although they do not usually cause severe illness.

subtypes.name: voiding symptoms
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May involve a weak or intermittent stream, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling or incomplete emptying.

subtypes.name: storage symptoms
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May involve urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence or nocturia.

subtypes.name: post-micturition symptoms
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Post-micturition dribbling is the principal symptom described.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify possible causes, associated conditions and medicines that might contribute to symptoms, including herbal and over-the-counter products.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial and specialist assessment.

diagnostic_workup.test: Physical examination, including abdomen, external genitalia and digital rectal examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess findings relevant to urological symptoms and other medical conditions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial and specialist assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An abnormal-feeling prostate is one reason to discuss PSA testing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record the pattern and volume of urination.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment for bothersome LUTS; at specialist assessment for LUTS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment.

Discuss the test and allow time for a decision if symptoms suggest bladder outlet obstruction secondary to BPE, the prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or the man is concerned about prostate cancer.

diagnostic_workup.test: Serum creatinine test and estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] calculation
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment only when renal impairment is suspected, for example with a palpable bladder, nocturnal enuresis, recurrent urinary tract infections or a history of renal stones.

diagnostic_workup.test: Flow-rate measurement and post-void residual volume measurement
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Specialist assessment; not routinely at initial assessment.
At specialist assessment, for example with a history of recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, haematuria, profound symptoms or pain; not routinely at initial assessment for uncomplicated LUTS.

diagnostic_workup.test: Imaging of the upper urinary tract
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At specialist assessment, for example with a history of chronic retention, haematuria, recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, profound symptoms or pain; not routinely at initial assessment for uncomplicated LUTS.
May be considered during specialist assessment if surgery is being contemplated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure the extent of urinary incontinence.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At specialist assessment only when quantification of incontinence is needed.

diagnostic_workup.test: Validated symptom score, for example the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish symptom severity before treatment so subsequent changes can be assessed.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering any treatment for LUTS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline defines mild as 0 to 7, moderate as 8 to 19 and severe as 20 to 35.

prognostic_tools.name: International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: The score categorises symptom severity and provides a baseline against which change after treatment can be assessed.

follow_up.schedule: Offer review if previously non-bothersome or uncomplicated symptoms change. Discuss regular follow-up when choosing active surveillance. For men taking alpha blockers, review at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months; for 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, at 3 to 6 months and then every 6 to 12 months; for anticholinergics, every 4 to 6 weeks until symptoms stabilise and then every 6 to 12 months.
recommended_tests: Assess symptoms, treatment effects on quality of life and adverse effects during drug-treatment reviews.

conditions.name: voiding LUTS
conditions.description: Lower urinary tract symptoms occurring during voiding; they may be presumed secondary to BPE when considering surgery.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible features include a weak or intermittent urinary stream, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling and incomplete emptying.

conditions.name: storage LUTS
conditions.description: Lower urinary tract symptoms related to urine storage.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Features include urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence and nocturia; urinary incontinence is particularly relevant to containment needs.

subtypes.name: urgency incontinence
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A form of urinary incontinence mentioned among storage symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During specialist assessment only if the extent of incontinence needs to be measured.

conditions.name: post-micturition dribble
conditions.description: The main post-micturition symptom identified by the guideline.
conditions.epidemiology: The symptom is described as common.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Dribbling after urination can be bothersome.

conditions.name: benign prostate enlargement (BPE)
conditions.description: Prostate enlargement associated with an increased number of prostate cells, termed benign prostatic hyperplasia, can obstruct the bladder outlet.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline identifies BPE causing bladder outlet obstruction as the most common cause of LUTS in men.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May produce LUTS suggestive of bladder outlet obstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the prostate during assessment of LUTS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial and specialist assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An abnormal-feeling prostate is an indication to discuss PSA testing.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Offer information, advice and time to decide about testing when LUTS suggest bladder outlet obstruction secondary to BPE.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A PSA level greater than 1.4 ng/ml is one criterion used in the guideline when considering a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor or its combination with an alpha blocker.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering treatments whose eligibility depends on prostate size.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline uses estimates larger than 30 g for certain drug options, smaller than 30 g for TUIP and larger than 80 g for open prostatectomy.

follow_up.schedule: For men taking alpha blockers, review at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months. For men taking 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, review at 3 to 6 months and then every 6 to 12 months.
recommended_tests: Assess symptoms, effects on quality of life and treatment-related adverse effects.

conditions.name: overactive bladder
conditions.description: A condition for which the guideline addresses management of storage LUTS and symptoms of overactive bladder.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Storage LUTS may be suggestive of overactive bladder.

follow_up.schedule: For men taking anticholinergics, review every 4 to 6 weeks until symptoms stabilise, then every 6 to 12 months.
recommended_tests: Assess symptoms, effects on quality of life and adverse effects from treatment.

conditions.name: nocturnal polyuria
conditions.description: A cause of nocturnal symptoms for which the guideline discusses treatment after consideration of other medical causes.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Nocturnal polyuria symptoms may also arise with diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, adrenal insufficiency, hypercalcaemia, liver failure, polyuric renal failure, chronic heart failure, obstructive apnoea, dependent oedema, pyelonephritis, chronic venous stasis or sickle cell anaemia. Calcium channel blockers, diuretics and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may also cause such symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude other medical causes before considering oral desmopressin.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When symptoms persist despite other treatments and oral desmopressin is being considered.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor sodium after starting oral desmopressin.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: 3 days after the first dose.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If serum sodium falls below the normal range, desmopressin treatment should be stopped.

follow_up.schedule: Measure serum sodium 3 days after the first dose of oral desmopressin.

conditions.name: stress urinary incontinence
conditions.description: A form of urinary incontinence addressed separately in the guideline's conservative and surgical management recommendations.

subtypes.name: stress urinary incontinence caused by prostatectomy
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The guideline specifies supervised pelvic floor muscle training for this group.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure the degree of urinary incontinence.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At specialist assessment only when measurement is needed.

follow_up.schedule: For incontinence caused by prostatectomy, continue pelvic floor muscle exercises for at least 3 months before considering other options.

conditions.name: detrusor overactivity
conditions.description: A condition for which the guideline discusses procedures when conservative management and drug treatment have not controlled symptoms.

conditions.name: acute urinary retention
conditions.description: Urinary retention requiring immediate catheterisation in the guideline.

conditions.name: chronic urinary retention
conditions.description: Persistent retention for which the guideline specifies assessment and management according to renal function, upper urinary tract findings, bladder function and symptom burden.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The assessment criteria given are a residual volume greater than 1 litre or a palpable or percussable bladder. Chronic retention may be associated with impaired renal function or hydronephrosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess retained urine and provide surveillance when the bladder has not been drained.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment or active surveillance of chronic retention.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A residual volume greater than 1 litre is one criterion specified for serum creatinine testing and upper urinary tract imaging.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When chronic retention involves a residual volume greater than 1 litre or a palpable or percussable bladder; also during active surveillance of non-bothersome LUTS secondary to chronic retention when the bladder has not been drained.

diagnostic_workup.test: Imaging of the upper urinary tract
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When chronic retention involves a residual volume greater than 1 litre or a palpable or percussable bladder; also during active surveillance of non-bothersome LUTS secondary to chronic retention when the bladder has not been drained.

follow_up.schedule: Provide active surveillance for men with non-bothersome LUTS secondary to chronic retention whose bladders have not been drained; no interval is specified.
recommended_tests: Imaging of the upper urinary tract.

therapies_index.name: lifestyle advice
approved_indications: Men with LUTS that are not bothersome or complicated
Men with storage LUTS suggestive of overactive bladder
Men choosing active surveillance for mild or moderate bothersome LUTS, or for LUTS that have not responded to drug treatment
therapies_index.administration: Advice may include fluid intake.

therapies_index.name: active surveillance
approved_indications: An option to discuss with men who have mild or moderate bothersome LUTS or whose LUTS have not responded to drug treatment
Men with non-bothersome LUTS secondary to chronic retention whose bladder has not been drained
therapies_index.administration: For bothersome LUTS, it consists of reassurance and lifestyle advice without immediate treatment, together with regular follow-up.
monitoring: For men with non-bothersome LUTS secondary to chronic retention whose bladder has not been drained: post-void residual volume measurement, upper tract imaging and serum creatinine testing.

therapies_index.name: urethral milking
approved_indications: Post-micturition dribble
therapies_index.administration: Explain to men how to perform the technique.

therapies_index.name: bladder training
approved_indications: Storage LUTS suggestive of overactive bladder
therapies_index.administration: Offer supervised training alongside advice on fluid intake and lifestyle, with containment products if needed. Inform men with proven bladder outlet obstruction that bladder training is less effective than surgery.

therapies_index.name: pelvic floor muscle training
approved_indications: Stress urinary incontinence caused by prostatectomy
therapies_index.administration: Offer supervised training and advise continuing the exercises for at least 3 months before considering other options.

therapies_index.name: containment products
approved_indications: Temporary social continence for storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, while diagnosis and management are being discussed
Management of storage LUTS according to individual circumstances and the man's preferences
Permanent use for storage LUTS only after assessment and exclusion of other management methods
therapies_index.administration: Offer a choice suited to the individual and provide products when needed.

therapies_index.name: pads
approved_indications: Temporary containment for storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence

therapies_index.name: absorbent pads
therapies_index.administration: Identified as a comparator with sheath collectors in proposed research involving men with urinary incontinence.

therapies_index.name: external collecting devices
approved_indications: Storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, before considering indwelling catheterisation
therapies_index.administration: Examples include sheath appliances and pubic pressure urinals.

therapies_index.name: sheath appliances
approved_indications: Containment of storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, before considering indwelling catheterisation

therapies_index.name: pubic pressure urinals
approved_indications: Containment of storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, before considering indwelling catheterisation

therapies_index.name: sheath collectors
therapies_index.administration: Identified as a comparator with absorbent pads in proposed research involving men with urinary incontinence.

therapies_index.name: penile clamps
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer for storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence.

therapies_index.name: intermittent bladder catheterisation
approved_indications: Voiding LUTS that cannot be corrected by less invasive measures; offer before indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheterisation

therapies_index.name: intermittent urethral catheterisation
approved_indications: Chronic urinary retention; consider self- or carer-administered catheterisation before an indwelling catheter
therapies_index.administration: May be performed by the man or a carer.

therapies_index.name: intermittent self- or carer-administered catheterisation
approved_indications: An option instead of surgery for chronic retention when markedly impaired bladder function is suspected
therapies_index.administration: Performed intermittently by the man or a carer.

therapies_index.name: indwelling urethral catheterisation
approved_indications: Consider long-term use for LUTS when medical management has failed, surgery is inappropriate, and the additional circumstances specified in the guideline apply
A catheterisation option to consider before surgery for chronic urinary retention
therapies_index.administration: Before offering long-term catheterisation, discuss practicalities, benefits and risks with the man and, where appropriate, his carer.

therapies_index.name: indwelling suprapubic catheterisation
approved_indications: An indwelling catheterisation option after intermittent bladder catheterisation has been considered for voiding LUTS that cannot be corrected by less invasive measures

therapies_index.name: long-term catheterisation
approved_indications: Continue or initiate for chronic retention when surgery is unsuitable

therapies_index.name: alpha blocker
approved_indications: Moderate to severe LUTS
Acute urinary retention before catheter removal
monitoring: Review at 4 to 6 weeks and subsequently every 6 to 12 months, assessing symptoms, quality-of-life effects and adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: alfuzosin
approved_indications: An alpha blocker offered for moderate to severe LUTS
monitoring: Review men taking alpha blockers at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months.

therapies_index.name: doxazosin
approved_indications: An alpha blocker offered for moderate to severe LUTS
monitoring: Review men taking alpha blockers at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months.

therapies_index.name: tamsulosin
approved_indications: An alpha blocker offered for moderate to severe LUTS
monitoring: Review men taking alpha blockers at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months.

therapies_index.name: terazosin
approved_indications: An alpha blocker offered for moderate to severe LUTS
monitoring: Review men taking alpha blockers at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months.

therapies_index.name: anticholinergic
approved_indications: Symptoms of overactive bladder
An additional treatment to consider when storage symptoms persist after an alpha blocker alone
monitoring: Review every 4 to 6 weeks until symptoms stabilise, then every 6 to 12 months; assess symptoms, quality-of-life effects and adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: beta-3-adrenoceptor agonists
approved_indications: The guideline points to NICE technology appraisal guidance for options to treat overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable side effects.

therapies_index.name: vibegron
approved_indications: The guideline refers to NICE technology appraisal guidance on its use for overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable side effects.

therapies_index.name: mirabegron
approved_indications: The guideline refers to NICE technology appraisal guidance on its use for overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable side effects.

therapies_index.name: 5-alpha reductase inhibitor
approved_indications: LUTS with a prostate estimated to be larger than 30 g or a PSA level greater than 1.4 ng/ml in men considered at high risk of progression
monitoring: Review at 3 to 6 months and subsequently every 6 to 12 months, assessing symptoms, quality-of-life effects and adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: a combination of an alpha blocker and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor
approved_indications: Consider for bothersome moderate to severe LUTS when the prostate is estimated to be larger than 30 g or PSA is greater than 1.4 ng/ml.
monitoring: Review alpha blocker treatment at 4 to 6 weeks and 5-alpha reductase inhibitor treatment at 3 to 6 months; subsequently review each every 6 to 12 months.

therapies_index.name: an anticholinergic as well as an alpha blocker
approved_indications: Consider when storage symptoms remain after treatment with an alpha blocker alone.
monitoring: Review anticholinergic treatment every 4 to 6 weeks until symptoms stabilise and then every 6 to 12 months; review alpha blocker treatment at 4 to 6 weeks and then every 6 to 12 months.

therapies_index.name: loop diuretic
approved_indications: Consider for nocturnal polyuria; the guideline states that loop diuretics did not have a UK marketing authorisation for this indication in June 2015.
therapies_index.administration: Late afternoon.

therapies_index.name: furosemide
approved_indications: Named as an example of a loop diuretic considered for nocturnal polyuria; the guideline states that loop diuretics did not have a UK marketing authorisation for this indication in June 2015.
therapies_index.administration: The loop diuretic option is offered in the late afternoon.

therapies_index.name: desmopressin
approved_indications: Consider for nocturnal polyuria after excluding other medical causes and when other treatments have not helped; the guideline states that it did not have a UK marketing authorisation for this indication in June 2015.
therapies_index.administration: Oral.
key_toxicities: Serum sodium may fall below the normal range.
monitoring: Measure serum sodium 3 days after the first dose; stop treatment if it is below the normal range.

therapies_index.name: phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer solely to treat LUTS in men except within a randomised controlled trial.

therapies_index.name: monopolar transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
approved_indications: A surgical option for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE when symptoms are severe or conservative management and drug treatment have been unsuccessful or are inappropriate

therapies_index.name: bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
approved_indications: A surgical option for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE when symptoms are severe or conservative management and drug treatment have been unsuccessful or are inappropriate

therapies_index.name: monopolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate (TUVP)
approved_indications: A surgical option for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE when symptoms are severe or conservative management and drug treatment have been unsuccessful or are inappropriate

therapies_index.name: holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP)
approved_indications: A surgical option for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE when symptoms are severe or conservative management and drug treatment have been unsuccessful or are inappropriate
therapies_index.administration: Perform at a centre specialising in the technique or with mentorship arrangements.

therapies_index.name: transurethral incision of the prostate (TUIP)
approved_indications: An alternative surgical option for men with voiding LUTS and a prostate estimated to be smaller than 30 g

therapies_index.name: open prostatectomy
approved_indications: An alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP only when the prostate is estimated to be larger than 80 g

therapies_index.name: transurethral needle ablation (TUNA)
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer as an alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE.

therapies_index.name: transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT)
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer as an alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE.

therapies_index.name: high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU)
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer as an alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE.

therapies_index.name: transurethral ethanol ablation of the prostate (TEAP)
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer as an alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE.

therapies_index.name: laser coagulation
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer as an alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin injection into the prostate
approved_indications: Consider for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE only within a randomised controlled trial.
therapies_index.administration: Injection into the prostate.

therapies_index.name: laser vaporisation techniques
approved_indications: Consider for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE only in a randomised controlled trial comparing the technique with TURP.

therapies_index.name: bipolar TUVP
approved_indications: Consider for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE only in a randomised controlled trial comparing it with TURP.

therapies_index.name: monopolar transurethral vaporisation resection of the prostate (TUVRP)
approved_indications: Consider for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE only in a randomised controlled trial comparing it with TURP.

therapies_index.name: bipolar transurethral vaporisation resection of the prostate (TUVRP)
approved_indications: Consider for voiding LUTS presumed secondary to BPE only in a randomised controlled trial comparing it with TURP.

therapies_index.name: cystoplasty
approved_indications: Consider for detrusor overactivity only after conservative management and drug treatment have failed, and only if the man is willing and able to self-catheterise.
therapies_index.administration: Before offering the procedure, discuss serious complications.
key_toxicities: Mucus production and/or mucus retention in the bladder

therapies_index.name: bladder wall injection with botulinum toxin
approved_indications: Consider for detrusor overactivity only when conservative management and drug treatment have failed and the man is willing and able to self-catheterise.
therapies_index.administration: Injection into the bladder wall.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin A
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned in connection with bladder wall injection for detrusor overactivity; the guideline states that it did not have a UK marketing authorisation for this indication in June 2015.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin B
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned in connection with bladder wall injection for detrusor overactivity; the guideline states that it did not have a UK marketing authorisation for this indication in June 2015.

therapies_index.name: implanted sacral nerve stimulation
approved_indications: Consider for detrusor overactivity only when conservative management and drug treatment have failed.

therapies_index.name: myectomy
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer to manage detrusor overactivity.

therapies_index.name: intramural injectables
approved_indications: Consider for stress urinary incontinence only as part of a randomised controlled trial.

therapies_index.name: implanted adjustable compression devices
approved_indications: Consider for stress urinary incontinence only as part of a randomised controlled trial.

therapies_index.name: male slings
approved_indications: Consider for stress urinary incontinence only as part of a randomised controlled trial.

therapies_index.name: retrobulbar 'non-compressive' male sling
therapies_index.administration: Named as an intervention for comparison in proposed research on mild to moderate post-prostatectomy urinary incontinence.

therapies_index.name: adjustable compression sling
therapies_index.administration: Named as an intervention for comparison in proposed research on mild to moderate post-prostatectomy urinary incontinence.

therapies_index.name: urinary diversion
approved_indications: Consider for intractable urinary tract symptoms only after conservative management and drug treatment have failed, and when cystoplasty or sacral nerve stimulation is clinically inappropriate or unacceptable to the patient.

therapies_index.name: implantation of an artificial sphincter
approved_indications: Consider for stress urinary incontinence only when conservative management and drug treatment have failed.

therapies_index.name: surgery on the bladder outlet
approved_indications: Consider without prior catheterisation for chronic urinary retention with other bothersome LUTS, provided renal function is not impaired and there is no upper renal tract abnormality.

therapies_index.name: homeopathy
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer for LUTS in men.

therapies_index.name: phytotherapy
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer for LUTS in men.

therapies_index.name: acupuncture
therapies_index.administration: Do not offer for LUTS in men.

recommendations.statement: At the initial assessment of men with LUTS, assess their medical history for possible causes and comorbidities, and review prescribed, herbal and over-the-counter medicines for potential contributors.
At initial assessment, offer an examination informed by urological symptoms and other conditions, including examination of the abdomen and external genitalia and a digital rectal examination.
At initial assessment, ask men with bothersome LUTS to complete a urinary frequency volume chart.
At initial assessment, offer urine dipstick testing for blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites.

At initial assessment, give men information, advice and time to decide about prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing if their LUTS suggest bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostate enlargement (BPE), their prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or they are worried about prostate cancer.
Manage suspected prostate cancer in men with LUTS according to the NICE guidelines on prostate cancer and suspected cancer.

At initial assessment, offer serum creatinine testing with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) calculation only when renal impairment is suspected, such as with a palpable bladder, nocturnal enuresis, recurrent urinary tract infections or a history of renal stones.
Do not routinely offer cystoscopy at initial assessment to men with uncomplicated LUTS, meaning LUTS without evidence of bladder abnormality.
Do not routinely offer upper urinary tract imaging at initial assessment to men with uncomplicated LUTS.
Do not routinely measure urinary flow rate at the initial assessment of men with LUTS.
Do not routinely measure post-void residual volume at the initial assessment of men with LUTS.

At initial assessment, reassure men whose LUTS are neither bothersome nor complicated, provide information about their condition and advice on lifestyle measures such as fluid intake, and offer reassessment if symptoms change.
Offer specialist referral to men whose bothersome LUTS have not improved with conservative management or drug treatment.

Refer men for specialist assessment when LUTS are complicated by recurrent or persistent urinary tract infection, retention, renal impairment suspected to result from lower urinary tract dysfunction, or suspected urological cancer.
Before any treatment for LUTS, offer assessment of baseline symptoms using a validated symptom score, such as the IPSS, so that subsequent changes can be evaluated.

During specialist assessment of men with LUTS, evaluate medical history for possible causes and comorbidities, and review current prescribed, herbal and over-the-counter medicines for potential contributors.

During specialist assessment, offer a physical examination directed by urological symptoms and other conditions, including examination of the abdomen and external genitalia and a digital rectal examination.
At specialist assessment, ask men with LUTS to complete a urinary frequency volume chart.

At specialist assessment, provide information, advice and time to decide about PSA testing when LUTS suggest bladder outlet obstruction due to BPE, the prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or the man is concerned about prostate cancer.
Offer flow-rate and post-void residual volume measurements to men undergoing specialist assessment for LUTS.
At specialist assessment, offer cystoscopy only when clinically indicated, for example by a history of recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, haematuria, profound symptoms or pain.

At specialist assessment, offer upper urinary tract imaging only when clinically indicated, for example by a history of chronic retention, haematuria, recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, profound symptoms or pain.
Consider multichannel cystometry during specialist assessment for men with LUTS who are contemplating surgery.
At specialist assessment, offer pad tests only when measurement of the extent of urinary incontinence is needed.
Teach men with post-micturition dribble how to carry out urethral milking.

Offer temporary containment products, such as pads or collecting devices, to men with storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, to support social continence while diagnosis and a management plan are being discussed.
Offer men a choice of containment products for storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, according to their circumstances and in consultation with them.
For storage LUTS suggestive of overactive bladder, offer supervised bladder training, guidance on fluid intake, lifestyle advice and containment products if required.
Tell men with LUTS and confirmed bladder outlet obstruction that bladder training is less effective than surgery.
Offer supervised pelvic floor muscle training for stress urinary incontinence caused by prostatectomy, and advise continuing the exercises for at least 3 months before considering other approaches.
Refer men with stress urinary incontinence for specialist assessment.
Do not offer penile clamps to men with storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence.
Before considering an indwelling catheter, offer external collecting devices, such as sheath appliances or pubic pressure urinals, to manage storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence.
For voiding LUTS that less invasive measures cannot correct, offer intermittent bladder catheterisation before an indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheter.

Consider long-term indwelling urethral catheterisation for men with LUTS when medical management has failed and surgery is inappropriate, and they cannot manage intermittent self-catheterisation, have urine-contaminated skin wounds, pressure ulcers or irritation, or are distressed by changes of bedding and clothing.
When offering long-term indwelling catheterisation, discuss its practical aspects, benefits and risks with the man and, when appropriate, his carer.
Explain that an indwelling catheter used for urgency incontinence might neither achieve continence nor relieve recurrent infections.
Consider permanent containment products for storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, only after assessment and exclusion of other management methods.
Offer drug treatment for bothersome LUTS only when conservative options have failed or are unsuitable.
When offering drug treatment for LUTS, account for the man's comorbidities and current treatment.
Offer an alpha blocker—alfuzosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin or terazosin—to men with moderate to severe LUTS.
Offer an anticholinergic for symptoms of overactive bladder in men.

For beta-3-adrenoceptor agonist options recommended in NICE technology appraisal guidance when antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable adverse effects, consult the guidance on vibegron (TA999, 2024) and mirabegron (TA290, 2013).

Offer a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor to men with LUTS who are considered at high risk of progression, such as older men, and whose prostate is estimated to be larger than 30 g or whose PSA exceeds 1.4 ng/ml.
Consider combining an alpha blocker with a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for bothersome moderate to severe LUTS when the prostate is estimated to be larger than 30 g or PSA is greater than 1.4 ng/ml.
Consider adding an anticholinergic for men whose storage symptoms persist despite an alpha blocker alone.
Consider a loop diuretic taken in the late afternoon for men with nocturnal polyuria.
recommendations.context: 1.4.9 [2010]; in June 2015, loop diuretics such as furosemide lacked UK marketing authorisation for this indication.

recommendations.statement: Consider oral desmopressin for nocturnal polyuria only after excluding other medical causes and when other treatments have not helped. Check serum sodium 3 days after the first dose, and stop desmopressin if it falls below the normal range.
recommendations.context: 1.4.10 [2010]; in June 2015, desmopressin lacked UK marketing authorisation for this indication. The guideline identifies diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, adrenal insufficiency, hypercalcaemia, liver failure, polyuric renal failure, chronic heart failure, obstructive apnoea, dependent oedema, pyelonephritis, chronic venous stasis and sickle cell anaemia as possible medical causes; calcium channel blockers, diuretics and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are possible medicine-related causes.

recommendations.statement: Do not offer phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors solely to treat LUTS in men, except within a randomised controlled trial.

Discuss active surveillance—reassurance and lifestyle advice with regular follow-up but no immediate treatment—or active intervention through conservative management, medicines or surgery with men who have mild or moderate bothersome LUTS or whose LUTS have not responded to drug treatment.
Review men receiving drug treatment for their symptoms, the medicines' effects on quality of life and any adverse effects.
Review men taking alpha blockers at 4 to 6 weeks and subsequently every 6 to 12 months.
Review men taking 5-alpha reductase inhibitors at 3 to 6 months and subsequently every 6 to 12 months.
Review men taking anticholinergics every 4 to 6 weeks until symptoms stabilise, then every 6 to 12 months.
Offer surgery for voiding symptoms only when they are severe or when drug treatment and conservative options have failed or are unsuitable; discuss surgical outcomes and alternatives.

If operating on voiding LUTS presumed due to BPE, offer monopolar or bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), monopolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate (TUVP), or holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP). Perform HoLEP in a centre specialising in the technique or with mentorship arrangements.
Offer transurethral incision of the prostate (TUIP) as an alternative surgical procedure for men whose prostate is estimated to be smaller than 30 g.
Offer open prostatectomy as an alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP only when the prostate is estimated to be larger than 80 g.

For surgery to manage voiding LUTS presumed due to BPE, do not offer minimally invasive treatments—including transurethral needle ablation (TUNA), transurethral microwave thermotherapy (TUMT), high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), transurethral ethanol ablation of the prostate (TEAP) and laser coagulation—as substitutes for TURP, TUVP or HoLEP.
For surgery to manage voiding LUTS presumed due to BPE, consider botulinum toxin injection into the prostate only within a randomised controlled trial.

For surgery to manage voiding LUTS presumed due to BPE, consider laser vaporisation techniques, bipolar TUVP, or monopolar or bipolar transurethral vaporisation resection of the prostate (TUVRP) only in a randomised controlled trial comparing them with TURP.

If offering surgery for storage symptoms, consider it only when conservative management and drug treatment have not worked. Discuss containment and surgery as alternatives, and explain that effectiveness, adverse effects and long-term risks remain uncertain.

When surgery for storage LUTS is being considered, refer the man to a urologist to discuss suitable surgical and non-surgical choices and each option's potential benefits and limitations, especially long-term outcomes.

Consider cystoplasty for detrusor overactivity only if conservative management or drug treatment has not worked and the man is willing and able to self-catheterise. First discuss serious complications: bowel disturbance, metabolic acidosis, mucus production and/or retention in the bladder, urinary tract infection and urinary retention.

Consider botulinum toxin injection into the bladder wall for detrusor overactivity only when conservative management and drug treatments have failed and the man is willing and able to self-catheterise.
recommendations.context: 1.6.4 [2010]; in June 2015, botulinum toxin A and botulinum toxin B lacked UK marketing authorisations for this indication.

recommendations.statement: Consider implanted sacral nerve stimulation for detrusor overactivity only after symptoms have failed to respond to conservative management and drug treatments.
Do not offer myectomy to manage detrusor overactivity in men.
Consider intramural injectables, implanted adjustable compression devices and male slings for stress urinary incontinence only within a randomised controlled trial.

Consider urinary diversion for intractable urinary tract symptoms only after conservative management and drug treatments have failed, and when cystoplasty or sacral nerve stimulation is clinically inappropriate or unacceptable to the man.
Consider implantation of an artificial sphincter for stress urinary incontinence only after conservative management and drug treatments have failed.
Catheterise men with acute retention immediately.
Offer an alpha blocker to men with acute urinary retention before removing the catheter.
For chronic urinary retention, consider intermittent urethral catheterisation performed by the man or a carer before offering an indwelling catheter.
Perform serum creatinine testing and upper urinary tract imaging in men with chronic urinary retention, defined here by residual volume greater than 1 litre or a palpable or percussable bladder.
Catheterise men whose chronic urinary retention has caused impaired renal function or hydronephrosis.
Consider intermittent or indwelling catheterisation before offering surgery for chronic urinary retention.

Consider bladder outlet surgery without prior catheterisation for men with chronic urinary retention and other bothersome LUTS when renal function is not impaired and the upper renal tract has no abnormality.
When markedly impaired bladder function is suspected in a man with chronic retention, consider intermittent catheterisation performed by the man or a carer instead of surgery.
Continue or initiate long-term catheterisation for men with chronic retention who are unsuitable for surgery.

For men with non-bothersome LUTS due to chronic retention whose bladder has not been drained, provide active surveillance with post-void residual volume measurement, upper tract imaging and serum creatinine testing.
Do not offer homeopathy, phytotherapy or acupuncture to treat LUTS in men.
Where appropriate, ensure carers are informed, involved in managing men's LUTS and able to provide feedback about treatments.
Ensure men with LUTS can access care addressing their emotional and physical conditions and relevant physical, emotional, psychological, sexual and social issues.
Provide containment products when needed to men with storage LUTS, particularly incontinence, and advise them about relevant support groups.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: This guideline addresses the management of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in men over 18. Its aim is to improve quality of life by identifying appropriate assessments and when conservative care, medicines or surgery may help.

document_sections.heading: Who is it for?
document_sections.content: The intended audiences are healthcare professionals, commissioners and providers, and men with LUTS together with their families or carers.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: People should participate in discussions and informed decisions about their care. The recommendations draw on the best available evidence; the full guideline describes the methods and evidence for the 2010 recommendations, and the addendum does so for the 2015 recommendations. In this guideline, an International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) of 0 to 7 denotes mild symptoms, 8 to 19 moderate symptoms and 20 to 35 severe symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Initial assessment
document_sections.content: Initial assessment may take place in any setting and is performed by a healthcare professional without specific training in managing LUTS in men. Offer a review of medical history, possible causes and comorbidities; examine current medicines, including herbal and over-the-counter products, for possible contributors. Offer an examination informed by urological symptoms and other conditions, including the abdomen, external genitalia and a digital rectal examination. Ask men with bothersome LUTS to complete a urinary frequency volume chart. Offer urine dipstick testing for blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites. Provide information, advice and time to decide about prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing if symptoms suggest bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostate enlargement (BPE), the prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or the man is concerned about prostate cancer. Manage suspected prostate cancer according to the NICE guidelines on prostate cancer and suspected cancer. Offer serum creatinine testing with estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] calculation only when renal impairment is suspected; examples include a palpable bladder, nocturnal enuresis, recurrent urinary tract infections or previous renal stones. Do not routinely offer cystoscopy or upper urinary tract imaging for uncomplicated LUTS at this stage, or routinely measure flow rate or post-void residual volume. For symptoms that are neither bothersome nor complicated, provide reassurance, information and lifestyle advice, such as advice about fluid intake, and offer review if symptoms change. Offer specialist referral when bothersome LUTS have not responded to conservative or drug treatment. Refer for specialist assessment when LUTS are complicated by recurrent or persistent urinary tract infection, retention, renal impairment suspected to arise from lower urinary tract dysfunction, or suspected urological cancer. Before any LUTS treatment, offer assessment of baseline symptoms with a validated score, such as IPSS, so subsequent changes can be assessed. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Specialist assessment
document_sections.content: Specialist assessment can occur in any setting but is performed by a healthcare professional specifically trained in managing LUTS in men. Offer a medical-history review covering possible causes, comorbidities and medicines, including herbal and over-the-counter products that might contribute. Offer an examination tailored to symptoms and other conditions, covering the abdomen, external genitalia and digital rectal examination. Ask men to complete a urinary frequency volume chart. Give information, advice and time to decide on PSA testing if symptoms suggest bladder outlet obstruction secondary to BPE, the prostate feels abnormal on digital rectal examination, or the man is concerned about prostate cancer. Offer flow-rate and post-void residual volume measurements. Offer cystoscopy only when clinically indicated, such as with a history of recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, haematuria, profound symptoms or pain. Offer upper urinary tract imaging only when clinically indicated, including a history of chronic retention, haematuria, recurrent infection, sterile pyuria, profound symptoms or pain. Consider multichannel cystometry if surgery is being contemplated. Offer pad tests only when urinary-incontinence severity needs quantification. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Conservative management
document_sections.content: Explain urethral milking to men with post-micturition dribble. For storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence, offer temporary containment products, such as pads or collecting devices, to provide social continence while diagnosis and management are discussed; offer a choice suited to the man's circumstances and preferences. For storage LUTS suggestive of overactive bladder, offer supervised bladder training, guidance on fluid intake, lifestyle advice and containment products if needed. Tell men with confirmed bladder outlet obstruction that bladder training is less effective than surgery. Offer supervised pelvic floor muscle training for stress urinary incontinence caused by prostatectomy, and advise continuing for at least 3 months before considering alternatives. Refer men with stress urinary incontinence for specialist assessment. Do not offer penile clamps for storage LUTS, particularly urinary incontinence. Offer external collecting devices, such as sheath appliances or pubic pressure urinals, before considering an indwelling catheter. For voiding LUTS that less invasive measures cannot correct, offer intermittent bladder catheterisation before indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheterisation. Consider long-term indwelling urethral catheterisation when medical management has failed and surgery is inappropriate, and the man cannot manage intermittent self-catheterisation, has urine-contaminated skin wounds, pressure ulcers or irritation, or is distressed by changes of bedding and clothing. If offering long-term indwelling catheterisation, discuss practical issues, benefits and risks with the man and, when appropriate, his carer. Explain that an indwelling catheter for urgency incontinence might not achieve continence or relieve recurrent infections. Consider permanent containment products only after assessment and exclusion of other management methods. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Drug treatment
document_sections.content: Offer medicines for bothersome LUTS only if conservative options have failed or are unsuitable, taking account of comorbidities and existing treatment. Offer an alpha blocker—alfuzosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin or terazosin—for moderate to severe LUTS, and offer an anticholinergic for overactive bladder symptoms. NICE technology appraisal guidance identifies beta-3-adrenoceptor agonist options when antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable adverse effects: vibegron (TA999, 2024) and mirabegron (TA290, 2013). Offer a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor when LUTS coexist with an estimated prostate size larger than 30 g or PSA greater than 1.4 ng/ml and a high risk of progression, for example in older men. Consider combining an alpha blocker and a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for bothersome moderate to severe LUTS with an estimated prostate size larger than 30 g or PSA greater than 1.4 ng/ml. Consider adding an anticholinergic if storage symptoms persist on an alpha blocker alone. Consider a late-afternoon loop diuretic for nocturnal polyuria; in June 2015, loop diuretics such as furosemide lacked UK marketing authorisation for this indication. Consider oral desmopressin for nocturnal polyuria only after excluding other medical causes and when other treatments have not helped. Check serum sodium 3 days after the first dose and stop desmopressin if it falls below the normal range. Potential medical causes of nocturnal polyuria symptoms include diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, adrenal insufficiency, hypercalcaemia, liver failure, polyuric renal failure, chronic heart failure, obstructive apnoea, dependent oedema, pyelonephritis, chronic venous stasis and sickle cell anaemia; possible medication causes include calcium channel blockers, diuretics and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). In June 2015, desmopressin lacked UK marketing authorisation for this indication. Do not offer phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors solely to treat LUTS in men except within a randomised controlled trial. The phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor recommendation is marked [new 2015]; the other dated drug-treatment recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: Review
document_sections.content: Discuss either active surveillance—reassurance and lifestyle guidance without immediate treatment, with regular follow-up—or active intervention through conservative measures, medicines or surgery with men who have bothersome mild or moderate LUTS and those whose LUTS do not respond to medicines. Review men receiving drug treatment for symptoms, effects on quality of life and adverse effects. Review alpha blocker treatment at 4 to 6 weeks and subsequently every 6 to 12 months; review 5-alpha reductase inhibitor treatment at 3 to 6 months and subsequently every 6 to 12 months. Review anticholinergic treatment every 4 to 6 weeks until symptoms stabilise, then every 6 to 12 months. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.5 Surgery for voiding symptoms
document_sections.content: Offer surgery for voiding symptoms only when they are severe or when conservative and drug options have failed or are inappropriate; discuss alternatives and surgical outcomes. If operating for voiding LUTS presumed due to BPE, offer monopolar or bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), monopolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate (TUVP), or holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP). HoLEP should be performed at a centre specialising in the technique or with mentorship arrangements. Offer transurethral incision of the prostate (TUIP) as another surgical option when the estimated prostate size is smaller than 30 g. Offer open prostatectomy as an alternative to TURP, TUVP or HoLEP only when the estimated prostate size is larger than 80 g. Do not offer minimally invasive treatments—transurethral needle ablation [TUNA], transurethral microwave thermotherapy [TUMT], high-intensity focused ultrasound [HIFU], transurethral ethanol ablation of the prostate [TEAP] or laser coagulation—as substitutes for TURP, TUVP or HoLEP in this setting. Consider injection of botulinum toxin into the prostate only within a randomised controlled trial. Consider laser vaporisation techniques, bipolar TUVP, or monopolar or bipolar transurethral vaporisation resection of the prostate (TUVRP) only within a randomised controlled trial comparing them with TURP. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.6 Surgery for storage symptoms
document_sections.content: If surgery is contemplated for storage symptoms, consider it only after conservative and drug treatments have failed. Discuss containment as an alternative and explain that effectiveness, adverse effects and long-term risks of surgery are uncertain. Refer men being considered for surgery for storage LUTS to a urologist to discuss appropriate surgical and non-surgical options and each option's possible benefits and limitations, particularly long-term outcomes. Consider cystoplasty for detrusor overactivity only after failure of conservative or drug treatment and only if the man is willing and able to self-catheterise. Before cystoplasty, discuss serious complications: bowel disturbance, metabolic acidosis, mucus production and/or retention in the bladder, urinary tract infection and urinary retention. Consider bladder wall injection with botulinum toxin for detrusor overactivity only after failure of conservative and drug treatments and if the man is willing and able to self-catheterise. In June 2015, botulinum toxin A and botulinum toxin B lacked UK marketing authorisations for this indication. Consider implanted sacral nerve stimulation for detrusor overactivity only after failure of conservative and drug treatments. Do not offer myectomy for detrusor overactivity. Consider intramural injectables, implanted adjustable compression devices and male slings for stress urinary incontinence only within a randomised controlled trial. Consider urinary diversion for intractable urinary tract symptoms only after failure of conservative and drug treatments and when cystoplasty or sacral nerve stimulation is clinically unsuitable or unacceptable to the patient. Consider an artificial sphincter implant for stress urinary incontinence only after failure of conservative and drug treatments. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.7 Treating urinary retention
document_sections.content: Catheterise men with acute retention immediately. Offer an alpha blocker for acute urinary retention before removing the catheter. For chronic urinary retention, consider intermittent urethral catheterisation performed by the man or a carer before indwelling catheterisation. Perform serum creatinine testing and upper urinary tract imaging when chronic retention involves residual volume greater than 1 litre or a palpable or percussable bladder. Catheterise men with renal impairment or hydronephrosis secondary to chronic retention. Consider intermittent or indwelling catheterisation before surgery. Consider bladder outlet surgery without prior catheterisation for chronic retention accompanied by other bothersome LUTS when renal function is unimpaired and the upper renal tract has no abnormality. If markedly impaired bladder function is suspected, consider self- or carer-administered intermittent catheterisation instead of surgery. Continue or initiate long-term catheterisation if surgery is unsuitable. For men with non-bothersome LUTS due to chronic retention whose bladder has not been drained, provide active surveillance using post-void residual measurements, upper tract imaging and serum creatinine testing. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.8 Alternative and complementary therapies
document_sections.content: Do not offer homeopathy, phytotherapy or acupuncture to treat LUTS in men. This recommendation is marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: 1.9 Providing information
document_sections.content: When appropriate, ensure carers receive information, participate in management and can provide feedback on treatment. Ensure men with LUTS can access care addressing their emotional and physical conditions, as well as relevant physical, emotional, psychological, sexual and social issues. Supply containment products when needed to men with storage LUTS, particularly incontinence, and advise them about relevant support groups. These recommendations are marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: Recommendations for research
document_sections.content: The guideline committee identifies research questions concerning multichannel cystometry, catheterisation, containment products, surgical devices for post-prostatectomy incontinence and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.

document_sections.heading: 1 Multichannel cystometry
document_sections.content: Research should determine the clinical and cost effectiveness of multichannel cystometry for improving patient-related outcomes among men considering bladder outlet surgery. This research question is marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: The proposed research could establish whether multichannel cystometry improves surgical outcomes by identifying patients with bladder outlet obstruction. A randomised controlled trial should compare preoperative multichannel cystometry with no intervention in men awaiting bladder outlet surgery.

document_sections.heading: 2 Catheterisation
document_sections.content: Research should compare the clinical and cost effectiveness and adverse events of intermittent catheterisation against indwelling suprapubic or urethral catheterisation in men with voiding difficulty and chronic urinary retention. This research question is marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: The number of men in this group is rising as the population ages and more radical prostatectomies are performed. UK practice varies considerably, without an established standard of good practice. Research could identify a more effective, patient-focused and cost-effective approach. A randomised controlled trial should compare intermittent, indwelling suprapubic and indwelling urethral catheterisation, assessing quality of life, healthcare resource use and adverse events, including leakage, skin breakdown, infection, erosion and death.

document_sections.heading: 3 Products for men with urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Research should compare absorbent pads with sheath collectors for men with urinary incontinence, addressing clinical and cost effectiveness and adverse events. This research question is marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: This population is increasing as radical prostatectomies become more frequent and the population ages. UK practice varies widely, with no established standard of good practice. Research could improve the effectiveness, patient focus and cost effectiveness of continence management. In current non-specialist practice, bladder training is often overlooked, and inadequate diagnosis can prevent optimal treatment of bladder dysfunction. Evidence-based product selection and management could improve quality of life, make more efficient use of skilled nurses or carers and reduce waste from unsuitable or suboptimal products. A randomised controlled trial should report symptom severity, quality of life, measured changes in leakage and adverse events.

document_sections.heading: 4 Male slings
document_sections.content: Research should assess the clinical and cost effectiveness of a male sling or implanted adjustable compression device in men with mild to moderate post-prostatectomy urinary incontinence, measuring symptom severity, quality of life, changes in measured leakage and adverse events. This research question is marked [2010].

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Guidance is needed on surgery for this growing group, for whom implantation of an artificial urinary sphincter was, until recently, the only acceptable treatment option. Many men consider that intervention too invasive or too susceptible to complications or failure and instead rely on containment. New interventions exist, but their comparative outcomes remain uncertain. Research could support clear recommendations and effective treatment for the majority of these men. The committee recommends a randomised controlled trial comparing up to three interventions: retrobulbar 'non-compressive' male sling, adjustable compression sling and implanted adjustable compression device.

document_sections.heading: 5 Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors
document_sections.content: The 2015 update added a research question about the clinical and cost effectiveness of phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5Is) for LUTS in men without erectile dysfunction. This question is marked [new 2015].

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Evidence is lacking on PDE5Is for men with LUTS who do not have erectile dysfunction; existing evidence includes men who have both conditions. Consequently, the standing committee considered a recommendation for routine clinical use inappropriate. Further evidence is needed before recommending PDE5Is for all men with LUTS, including those without erectile dysfunction. A randomised controlled trial should compare PDE5Is with usual care in men over 45 years who have LUTS without erectile dysfunction. Outcomes should include International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) symptoms, IPSS quality of life, maximal urinary flow, residual urine volume, postural hypotension, headaches and withdrawals due to adverse events.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: LUTS encompass storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms. Possible causes involve abnormal structure or function of the prostate, urethra, bladder or sphincters. In men, the most common cause is benign prostate enlargement (BPE), which obstructs the bladder outlet; BPE arises from an increase in prostate cell numbers called benign prostatic hyperplasia. Other possible causes include detrusor weakness or overactivity, prostate inflammation (prostatitis), urinary tract infection, prostate cancer and neurological disease. Categorising symptoms as voiding, storage or post-micturition helps identify their source. Voiding symptoms comprise a weak or intermittent stream, straining, hesitancy, terminal dribbling and incomplete emptying. Storage symptoms comprise urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence and nocturia. Post-micturition dribbling is the main post-micturition symptom and is common and bothersome. LUTS usually do not cause severe illness but can substantially impair quality of life or indicate serious urogenital disease. They impose a major burden on ageing men: age is an important risk factor, prevalence rises with age, and bothersome LUTS occur in up to 30% of men older than 65 years. This represents a large population that might need treatment.

document_sections.heading: Update information
document_sections.content: The June 2015 update added a drug-treatment recommendation and a research recommendation concerning phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors. The label [new 2015] denotes a recommendation added or updated after an evidence review; [2010] denotes one whose evidence has not been reviewed since 2010.
